input.statement: The closest work evaluates with structured multiple-choice items generated over its own disease-specific KG/CG datasets across 1-5 hops, and reports robustness to option shuffling with an average absolute accuracy change below one percentage point.

the QA performance drops dramatically when the subgraph includes more than 5,000 nodes

We adopt three benchmark datasets for the multi-hop KBQA task: MetaQA [38] contains more than 400k single and multi-hop (up to 3-hop) questions in the domain of movie, containing three datasets, namely MetaQA-1hop, MetaQA-2hop and MetaQA-3hop.

input.statement: The standard multi-hop KBQA evaluation regime measures answer-entity ranking (Hits@1, and F1 in the retrieval work) on WebQSP and CWQ over Freebase-like KGs, while the intermediate-supervision work uses MetaQA (1/2/3-hop), WebQSP and CWQ; these benchmarks carry naturally occurring questions and no source-passage provenance, and their deepest standard multi-hop tier is 3 hops.

evidence.quote: the QA performance drops dramatically when the subgraph includes more than 5,000 nodes
after option shuffling, the average absolute change remains below one percentage point across models

input.statement: The two evaluation regimes are not interchangeable, so replication of the context-supervision effect under standard-benchmark methodology is untested rather than likely or unlikely. The closest work's metric is four-way answer selection over synthetically generated options whose hop depth is controlled by construction, on KGs built for the purpose; the standard regime is Hits@1 entity ranking on naturally occurring questions over Freebase with no passage provenance. A selection-accuracy gain among four generated options need not appear in Hits@1 ranking, and the standard benchmarks cannot host the mechanism at all because their triples are not traceable to source passages; conversely, the standard regime's deepest standard tier is 3 hops, whereas the idea's claim is specifically about 3-5 hops. The appropriate methodology for the refined question is therefore per-hop accuracy on a frozen split plus open-ended exact match/F1 on a text-attributed corpus, retaining multiple choice only for comparability with the published number.

input.confidence_basis: Based on verified quotes describing each side's evaluation protocol (synthetic per-hop MCQ with option shuffling versus Hits@1/F1 on WebQSP, CWQ and up-to-3-hop MetaQA) and on the earlier finding that benchmark KGs lack passage provenance; no paper directly tests cross-regime transfer, so the transfer question itself remains unmeasured.
input.resolution: Narrowed, not settled. The closest work's methodology is four-way multiple-choice accuracy over synthetically generated items spanning 1-5 hops on two purpose-built disease KGs, with option-shuffling robustness below one percentage point; the standard multi-hop regime is Hits@1 (and F1) answer-entity ranking on WebQSP and CWQ over Freebase-like graphs, with the deepest standard multi-hop tier being 3-hop MetaQA and no source-passage provenance. These measure different things (option selection among generated distractors versus entity ranking on natural questions) on different data, and the mechanism cannot even be instantiated on the standard benchmarks without passage-attributed KGs; so replication under the standard methodology is untested rather than expected. The comparison supports a mixed protocol for the refined question - per-hop accuracy on a frozen split plus open-ended exact match/F1 on a text-attributed corpus, with multiple choice retained only for comparability - and leaves the cross-metric transfer question (recorded separately) to be measured.

input.description: The published context-over-KG advantage is measured only as four-way multiple-choice accuracy over generated options whose distractors come from the same KG/CG. Option selection can be easier than free-form answer generation: a model may benefit from context when discriminating among four candidates without being able to produce the answer entity string. Whether the same context effect survives under open-ended exact match/F1 on the same items is unmeasured, so the size (and possibly the sign) of the effect under the metric the refined question proposes is unknown.
input.question: Do multiple-choice gains from context-augmented supervision transfer to open-ended exact match/F1 on the same questions, or does the multiple-choice format inflate the apparent effect?
input.rationale: If the effect is largely a discrimination effect, the practical claim and the comparison with generation-based KGQA systems weaken; the experiment is inexpensive to add (same checkpoints, re-scored with open-ended prompts) and directly affects how the refined contribution should be stated.
